## Numerical Quadrature

Numerical quadrature refers to numerically approximating a definite integral:
$$A = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx, \qquad a, b \text{ finite}$$

Note that if $a, b$ are not finite, we need to do a transformation first.

For example, let
$$\theta = t(x) = \log\frac{x}{1-x} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad x = t^{-1}(\theta) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-\theta}}$$

If $a=-\infty$, $b=+\infty$, then
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^1 f\!\left(t^{-1}(\theta)\right) dt^{-1}(\theta)$$

![](Lec%2008%20numerical%20quadrature_images/p001-fig.png)

## Example: Logistic Transformation

The logistic function maps the whole real line onto $(0,1)$:
$$y = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}, \qquad x = \log\left(\frac{y}{1-y}\right) = t(y)$$

Using this as a change of variables,
$$\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^1 f(t(y))\, t'(y)\, dy$$

Define $g(y) = f(t(y))\, t'(y)$. The transformed integrand $g(y)$ is now supported on the finite interval $(0,1)$, so it is amenable to numerical quadrature.

![](Lec%2008%20numerical%20quadrature_images/p002-fig.png)

## Calculating a Probability

For the standard normal density
$$\varphi(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\, e^{-\frac{x^2}{2}}$$
the probability that $X$ falls in $(a,b)$ is
$$P(a < X < b) = \int_a^b \varphi(x)\,dx$$

Define the truncated density
$$\varphi^{(t)}(x) = \varphi(x)\, I(a < x < b)$$
so that this probability is the area under $\varphi^{(t)}(x)$, shown shaded below.

![](Lec%2008%20numerical%20quadrature_images/p003-fig.png)

## Riemann Rule

Partition $[a,b]$ into $n$ equal sub-intervals of width
$$h_n = \frac{b-a}{n}$$

The Riemann-sum approximation to the integral is
$$\widetilde A_n = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} h_n \cdot f(a + i\,h_n)$$

with
$$\text{error} = O\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)$$

![](Lec%2008%20numerical%20quadrature_images/p004-fig.png)

## Midpoint Rule and Trapezoidal Rule

**Midpoint Rule.** With $h_n = (b-a)/n$,
$$\widetilde A_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} h_n \cdot f\!\left(a + \left(i - \tfrac12\right) h_n\right), \qquad \text{error} = O\!\left(\frac1n\right)$$

**Trapezoidal Rule.** With $x_0 = a$, $x_1 = a + h_n$, and $h_n = (b-a)/n$, on a single sub-interval
$$\widetilde A_1 = \tfrac12\big(f(x_0) + f(x_1)\big)\cdot (x_1 - x_0)$$

Summing over all sub-intervals:
$$\widetilde A_n = \tfrac12 h_n\Big[f(a) + f(a+h_n) + f(a+h_n) + \cdots + f(a+(n-1)h_n) + f(a+(n-1)h_n) + f(b)\Big]$$
$$= \tfrac12 h_n\big[f(a) + f(b)\big] + h_n \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} f(a + i\,h_n)$$

![](Lec%2008%20numerical%20quadrature_images/p005-fig.png)

## Simpson's Rule

Let $n = 2m$ be even and $h_n = (b-a)/n$. On $[x_0,x_1]$, approximate $f$ by a quadratic $\tilde f$ matching $f$ at $x_0$, the midpoint, and $x_1$:
$$\int_{x_0}^{x_1} f(x)\,dx \approx \frac{x_1-x_0}{6}\left[f(x_0) + 4\hat f\!\left(\frac{x_0+x_1}{2}\right) + f(x_1)\right] = (x_1-x_0)\left[\tfrac16 f(x_0) + \tfrac46 \hat f\!\left(\tfrac{x_0+x_1}{2}\right) + \tfrac16 f(x_1)\right]$$

Applying this on every pair of sub-intervals from $a$ to $b$:
$$\widehat A_{2m} = \frac{2h_n}{6}\Big[f(a) + 4f(a+h_n) + f(a+2h_n) + f(a+2h_n) + 4f(a+3h_n) + f(a+4h_n) + f(a+4h_n) + 4f(a+5h_n) + f(a+6h_n) + \cdots + f(b-2h_n) + 4f(b-h_n) + f(b)\Big]$$

$$= \frac{h_n}{3}\left[f(a) + f(b) + 4\sum_{i=1}^{m} f(a+(2i-1)h_n) + 2\sum_{i=1}^{m-1} f(a+2i\,h_n)\right]$$

![](Lec%2008%20numerical%20quadrature_images/p006-fig.png)

## An Example of Computing Marginalized Likelihood

We demonstrated the midpoint rule with a simple example.

**Example** (Normal data with log-norm prior for $\sigma$). The data $X_1,\dots,X_n$ are modelled as IID samples from a normal distribution given the value of the mean parameter $\mu$ and the logarithm of the standard deviation $\sigma$, denoted by $w$. The likelihood function of $\mu$ and $w$ based on data $X_1,\dots,X_n$ is therefore:
$$L(\mu,w) = \prod_{i=1}^n \phi(x_i;\mu,e^w)$$
where $\phi(x;\mu,\sigma)$ is the density function of a Normal distribution with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.

We assign normal priors to parameters $\mu$ and $w$, with fixed $\mu_0,\sigma_\mu,w_0,\sigma_w$:
$$\mu \sim N(\mu_0,\sigma_\mu), \qquad w \sim N(w_0,\sigma_w)$$

The density function of the prior for $\mu$ and $w$ is therefore:
$$P(\mu,w) = \phi(\mu;\mu_0,\sigma_\mu)\,\phi(w;w_0,\sigma_w)$$

The posterior distribution of $\mu$ and $w$ can be found using Bayes' rule:
$$P(\mu,w \mid X_1,\dots,X_n) = \frac{L(\mu,w)\,P(\mu,w)}{\int_\mu \int_w L(\mu,w)\,P(\mu,w)\,d\mu\,dw}$$

We will want to compute the normalizing constant $\int_\mu \int_w L(\mu,w)\,P(\mu,w)\,d\mu\,dw$, which is needed to compare this model with other models. Since this integral is intractable, we will use the midpoint rule to approximate it. The ranges of $\mu$ and $w$ are both infinite, so we apply the following change of variables to $\mu$ and $w$ before applying the midpoint rule:
$$\mu(\mu_t) = \log(\mu_t) - \log(1-\mu_t), \qquad w(w_t) = \log(w_t) - \log(1-w_t)$$

We then compute the following integral for the normalizing constant:
$$\int_{\mu_t} \int_{w_t} L\big(\mu(\mu_t), w(w_t)\big)\, P\big(\mu(\mu_t), w(w_t)\big)\, \frac{1}{\mu_t(1-\mu_t)}\, \frac{1}{w_t(1-w_t)}\, d\mu_t\, dw_t$$

## Marginal Likelihood

For data $y$ and parameter $\theta$ with likelihood $L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n P(y_i\mid\theta)$ and prior $\pi(\theta)$, the marginal likelihood (evidence) is
$$P(y) = \int L(\theta)\,\pi(\theta)\,d\theta = E_\pi\big[L(\theta)\big] = \int \prod_{i=1}^n P(y_i\mid\theta)\, \pi(\theta)\, d\theta$$

and the posterior is
$$P(\theta \mid y) = \frac{\prod_{i=1}^n P(y_i\mid\theta)\,\pi(\theta)}{P(y)}$$

![](Lec%2008%20numerical%20quadrature_images/p008-fig.png)

## Example: Normal Mean and Log-Variance

$$Y_1,\dots,Y_n \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$$
$$\mu \sim \pi_\mu(\mu), \qquad \mu \sim N(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2)$$
$$\sigma^2 \sim \pi_{\sigma^2}(\sigma^2), \qquad w = \log\sigma^2 \sim N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)$$

The marginal likelihood is
$$ML = \iint \left[\prod_{i=1}^n P(y_i \mid \mu,\sigma^2)\right] \pi(\mu)\,\pi(\sigma^2)\; d\mu\, d\sigma^2 = \iint f(\mu,\sigma^2)\, d\mu\, d\sigma^2$$

![](Lec%2008%20numerical%20quadrature_images/p009-fig.png)

## Transformation for the Midpoint Rule

To handle the infinite range of $\mu$, use the logistic transform:
$$\mu_t = \frac{1}{1+e^{-\mu}} \in (0,1), \qquad \mu = \log\left(\frac{\mu_t}{1-\mu_t}\right)$$

with
$$d\mu = d\left[\log\left(\frac{\mu_t}{1-\mu_t}\right)\right]$$

To average the (log-)integrand values on the transformed grid, we work on the log scale for numerical stability:
$$\log \sum_{i=1}^{4} e^{\log f(x_i)}$$

![](Lec%2008%20numerical%20quadrature_images/p010-fig.png)

## Two-Dimensional Midpoint Rule

For a two-parameter integral, the midpoint rule extends to a grid over $(\mu_t, w_t) \in (0,1) \times (0,1)$: the integrand $f(\mu_t, w_t)$ is evaluated at the midpoint of every grid cell, and the double integral is approximated by summing $f$ over the grid weighted by the cell area.

![](Lec%2008%20numerical%20quadrature_images/p011-fig.png)

## Marginal Likelihood via the Midpoint Rule

$$ML = \int L(\theta)\, \pi(\theta)\, d\theta$$

The figure below illustrates the likelihood $L(\theta)$, the prior $\pi(\theta)$ (e.g., a $N(0,10^2)$ prior), and their product $L(\theta)\pi(\theta)$, whose area under the curve is approximated by the midpoint rule on a grid of $\theta$.

![](Lec%2008%20numerical%20quadrature_images/p012-fig.png)

## Difficulty of Numerical Quadrature

We want to compute $\int f(x)\,dx$ over $(a,b)$.

A smooth, wide function is well approximated by a coarse grid. But if $f$ has a sharp, narrow peak relative to the grid spacing, most grid points can miss the peak entirely and the quadrature rule badly underestimates the integral — as illustrated by the tall spike hidden between grid points below.

![](Lec%2008%20numerical%20quadrature_images/p013-fig.png)

## Difficulty of Numerical Quadrature in High Dimensions

The same problem is far worse in high dimensions. A grid over $(\theta_1,\theta_2)$ must be fine enough to resolve a small concentrated contour region of the integrand, and as the dimension $r$ grows, the fraction of the grid that lands near where the integrand actually has mass shrinks sharply — the required number of grid points grows exponentially with dimension.

![](Lec%2008%20numerical%20quadrature_images/p014-fig.png)

## Example: Marginal Likelihood via Logistic Transform

Recall the logistic transform used to map an infinite-range parameter $\mu$ to $(0,1)$:
$$\mu_t = \frac{1}{1+e^{-\mu}}, \qquad \mu = \log\left(\frac{\mu_t}{1-\mu_t}\right)$$

Applying the midpoint rule on the $\mu_t$ grid approximates integrals such as the normalized posterior density
$$\frac{\pi(\theta)\,L(\theta)}{\int \pi(\theta)\,L(\theta)\,d\theta}$$

![](Lec%2008%20numerical%20quadrature_images/p015-fig.png)
